# 2 Maccabees Chapter 9 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 9 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_009_page_001.jpg

---

**9:1** About that time, Antiochus made his retreat in disgrace from the regions of Persia.

**9:2** He had entered the city called Persepolis and attempted to rob the temple and to seize control of the city. But the populace rose up in arms to defend themselves, and as a result Antiochus was routed by the inhabitants and forced to withdraw in humiliation.

**9:3** While he was in Ecbatana, word reached him of what had happened to Nicanor and to the forces of Timothy.

**9:4** Overcome with rage, he conceived a plan to make the Jews pay for the injury inflicted by those who had driven him back. He therefore commanded his charioteer to drive without ceasing until the journey was complete. Yet heaven's judgment was already riding with him; for in his arrogance he had declared: "When I reach there I will make Jerusalem a mass grave of Jews."

**9:5** But the all-seeing Lord, the God of Israel, struck him with an invisible and incurable blow. As soon as he uttered those words, an irremediable pain seized his bowels and sharp torments within his belly.

**9:6** And fittingly so — for he had tormented the bowels of others with many and strange cruelties.

**9:7** Yet he did not cease his arrogance in the slightest; instead, his pride swelled even greater. Breathing out fire in his fury against the Jews, he gave orders to press on. But it came to pass that he fell from his chariot as it was careering along, and was thrown violently so that every joint of his body was wrenched by the fall.

**9:8** So the man who had boasted in his superhuman arrogance that he could give orders to the waves of the sea and weigh the mountains on a balance was now laid low, being carried in a litter — a demonstration of the power of God manifest to all.

**9:9** And worms swarmed up out of the body of this impious man, and while he was still alive in agony and pain his flesh began to rot away, and because of the stench the entire army found the decomposition nauseating.

**9:10** The man who a short time before had thought himself able to reach the stars of heaven, no one could endure to transport on account of the unbearable stench.

**9:11** Then at last, having been broken in spirit, he began to come down from his great arrogance, brought to his senses under the scourging of God, since he was tormented by pain at every moment.

**9:12** And when he could no longer endure his own stench, he said: "It is just to be subject to God, and one who is mortal ought not to entertain thoughts equal to those of God."

**9:13** And this vile man made vows to the Lord, who would show him no more mercy, in the following terms:

**9:14** that the holy city, toward which he had been hastening in order to raze it to the ground and to turn it into a mass grave, he would declare to be free;

**9:15** and the Jews, whom he had resolved not even to count worthy of burial but to hand over to the birds and to the wild animals along with their infants, he would make equal to the Athenian citizens;

**9:16** and the holy sanctuary, which he had previously plundered, he would adorn with the finest votive offerings; and the sacred vessels he would restore multiplied many times over; and the costs of the sacrifices he would supply from his own revenues;

**9:17** and in addition to all this he would himself become a Jew and travel through every inhabited region announcing the might of God.

**9:18** But since his sufferings did not let up in the slightest — for the just judgment of God had overtaken him — having despaired of his own survival, he wrote to the Jews the letter reproduced below, having the form of a supplication. It read as follows:

**9:19** "To the worthy Jewish citizens, Antiochus the king and general, many greetings and wishes for health and prosperity.

**9:20** If you and your children are well, and your affairs proceed as you wish, I render very great thanks to God, my hope being in heaven.

**9:21** As for myself, I lie ill in body; yet I recall with fondness the honor and goodwill you showed me. As I return from the regions of Persia, having fallen ill with a troublesome sickness, I judged it necessary to give thought to the common welfare of all.

**9:22** I do not despair of my condition — for I have good hope of recovering from my illness —

**9:23** but observing that my father also, whenever he campaigned in the upper regions, appointed his successor,

**9:24** so that if anything unforeseen occurred or any difficult report arrived, those throughout the land, knowing to whom the government had been left, would not be thrown into confusion,

**9:25** and in view further of the fact that the neighboring princes, the neighbors and kinsmen of my kingdom, are on the watch for opportunities — I have constituted as king my son Antiochus, whom I have frequently entrusted to most of you when I was making hurried journeys to the upper provinces. I have written to him what I set down below.

**9:26** I therefore urge and beseech you to remember the public and private benefits you have received and to maintain each of you your goodwill toward me and my son.

**9:27** For I am persuaded that he will deal with you with gentleness and kindness, following my purpose in being well disposed toward you."

**9:28** Thus the murderer and blasphemer, having endured the most terrible suffering, such as he had inflicted on others, met his death in a most miserable fashion among the mountains in a foreign land.

**9:29** Philip, his foster brother, conveyed the body home; but then, fearing the son of Antiochus, he withdrew to Ptolemy Philometor in Egypt.
